A 19th-century academic oil painting with a smooth, finely blended surface: soft glazed transitions, delicate fine detail, minimal visible brushstrokes, no heavy impasto, no rough texture. Strong light and shadow from a single warm source (a lamp, a torch, a fire, a low sun) or from heavy overcast, with deep chiaroscuro. Palette of umber, ochre, gold, olive and near-black, with occasional cool accents. The manner of a romantic landscape, a grand historical scene, or a natural-history study of a creature painted as if real. A low, close viewpoint. Wet, reflective stone where there is stone; ancient architecture where there is architecture; one saturated subject held against darkness; scale shown by something small beside something vast. Quiet, watchful, ominous mood. No text, no lettering, no border, no frame, no grid texture, not photographic.

A grand historical scene: the crowded hall of a long clay-walled, reed-roofed house, in the daytime in the wet of winter under heavy overcast, seen from low among the townspeople standing packed at the back of the hall, just inside its one open door, looking up the length of the room. The only light is the grey daylight that comes in through the open door behind the viewer: it falls down the middle of the beaten clay floor, catches wet shoulders and wet hair, and leaves the clay walls and the underside of the reed roof in near-black. In the middle of the hall eleven people of the town sit in a ring on the floor, men and women, most of them dark shapes with the light on a shoulder, a hand or a grey head, their faces turned toward one standing figure or lost in shadow. At the foot of the ring, nearest the viewer and with its back to the door, stands the one figure the daylight reaches fully. A tall, lean figure in a long coat with many deep pockets, the coat the first thing seen. The face is a middle-aged mortal's, plain, with steady eyes that watch as a man watches a scale while the pans settle. The hands are stained with ink and green verdigris. A pair of small, plain brass scales, slightly dented, hangs at the belt. Seen from behind or in deep shadow, the head turned away or lost in darkness, no face visible. Here the figure stands still and upright with its stained hands open at its sides, speaking to the ring, the daylight on the back of the long coat and on the brass at the belt. All around the walls and behind the viewer the townspeople stand shoulder to shoulder, silent, wiry, sun-dark boat people, broad, stocky people in clay-stained clothes, weathered, quiet people, a few tall, pale people, and more heads crowd the doorway. Close to the viewer, at the edge of the open floor, a small child held on its mother's hip is looking at the standing figure. By the far wall, almost in darkness, a plank bench and a wooden weighing beam hung on a cord with two shallow pans of fired clay. No metal armor, no stone walls, no windows, no weapons raised. The one tall dark figure and the small child, in the wide silent crowd and the black depth of the hall, give the scale.
